This directory contains scripts and configuration for using [GAM](https://github.com/GAM-team/GAM) to manage CYC
Community Sailing Center's Google Workspace account.

`packages/gsuite-sync` syncs group membership, managers, owners, and settings from the CRM. Use
these scripts only as the break-glass path when that job is broken: read back live state with
`export-groups`/`export-group-members`, or apply a settings template by hand with
`apply-templates` if the Groups Settings API rejects the job's service account.

## Environment Variables

The scripts in this directory utilize environment variables for configuration, which are automatically set by devenv:

- `GAM_ADMIN_USER`: The user that GAM operates under (set in `devenv.nix`)
- `GAM_SPREADSHEET_ID`: ID of the spreadsheet to read batch commands from (set in `devenv.nix`)

## Setup

GAM requires a GCP project with a service account for domain-wide delegation, and an OAuth token for the admin user.

### Using an existing service account

If a service account already exists in the GCP project, you can reuse it by creating a new key:

1. Go to the [GCP Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/) and navigate to **IAM & Admin > Service Accounts**.
2. Find the GAM service account and create a new JSON key.
3. Download the key and move it to `~/.config/gam/oauth2service.json`.

### Setting up a new project

If you need to create a new project or re-initialize the service account credentials:

```bash
just use-project
```

This will open a browser for Google OAuth and create `client_secrets.json` and `oauth2service.json` in `~/.config/gam/`.

### Verifying the service account

After setting up the service account, verify it has the required API scopes for domain-wide delegation:

```bash
just check
```

This will list any missing scopes and provide a link to authorize them in the Google Admin console.

### Authenticating

Once the service account is configured, authenticate as the admin user:

```bash
just auth
```

## Scripts

### apply-templates

Applies group settings from a template file for each group listed in the "Group Templates" worksheet of `GAM_SPREADSHEET_ID`.

**Usage:**

```bash
./scripts/apply-templates
```

**Spreadsheet columns:**

- `Email`: The group email address
- `Template`: Path to the template JSON file (relative to `templates/` directory)

### export-groups

Exports all Google Groups (name, description, and settings) to the "Groups Export" worksheet in `GAM_SPREADSHEET_ID`.

**Usage:**

```bash
./scripts/export-groups
```

### export-group-members

Exports all group members across all groups to the "Groups Members Export" worksheet in `GAM_SPREADSHEET_ID`.

**Usage:**

```bash
./scripts/export-group-members
```

## Templates

The JSON files in the `templates` directory contain group settings to apply to different types of groups. See the [GAM Cheat Sheet](https://gamcheatsheet.com/GAM%20Cheat%20Sheet%20A4.pdf) for more details on group settings.

The same four templates also live in `packages/gsuite` (`group-settings-templates.ts`), which is what `gsuite-sync`'s settings pass applies day to day - these files are only the break-glass path `apply-templates` reads. Keep the two copies in step: a change here belongs there too, and vice versa.

### announcement.json

**Use case:** Announcement-only groups where only managers can post.

**Key settings:**

- Only managers and owners can post messages
- All members can view messages
- No collaborative inbox
- Messages are archived

### crew.json

**Use case:** Collaborative team groups where all members actively participate.

**Key settings:**

- Anyone can post messages (internal and external)
- Members can post as the group
- Members have permissions to manage topics, mark favorites, assist with content
- Messages are archived

### inbox.json

**Use case:** Shared inbox for team collaboration with inbox-style organization.

**Key settings:**

- Collaborative inbox enabled
- Anyone can post messages
- Members can moderate content, delete posts, manage topics
- Default sender is the group (not individual)
- Messages are archived

### participants.json

**Use case:** Program participant groups where members can communicate but management is restricted.

**Key settings:**

- All members can post messages
- Only managers can moderate, manage members, or perform administrative tasks
- Messages are archived
- Not shown in group directory

## Common Commands

See the [GAM Cheat Sheet](https://gamcheatsheet.com/GAM%20Cheat%20Sheet%20A4.pdf) for more commands.

### Managing Groups

Clear all members from a group (e.g., at the start of a season):

```bash
gam update group <group-email> clear member
```

### Working with Templates

Create a template based on an existing group:

```bash
gam info group "<group-email>" noaliases nousers formatjson > "<template-path>"
```

Apply a template to a group:

```bash
gam update group "<group-email>" json file "<template-path>"
```

## 7. Deployer identity and access (bootstrap)

Done as a Workspace **super-admin**, granting a human, not code, since these are IAM-policy grants
on the org's and project's break-glass access.

- [ ] `roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin` on the org, so the deployer can manage IAM without
      super-admin credentials.
- [ ] `roles/owner` on project `cyc-admin-scripts`, so `pulumi up` (including bootstrap) works.
- [ ] `roles/compute.osLoginExternalUser` on the org, for IAP SSH (`just ssh`, `just logs`,
      `just db-tunnel`) — required because Owner doesn't cover OS Login for an external principal.

```sh
gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding <ORG_ID> --member="user:<deployer-email>" --role="roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin" --condition=None
gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding <ORG_ID> --member="user:<deployer-email>" --role="roles/compute.osLoginExternalUser" --condition=None
```

Google refuses `roles/owner` for an external principal over the API. Grant it in the
[IAM console](https://console.cloud.google.com/iam-admin/iam?project=cyc-admin-scripts) instead:
add the principal, role **Basic → Owner**, then have them accept the emailed invitation.

**One correction to #152**, since I filed it before reading the client docs: I flagged `MCP_OAUTH_DCR_ENABLED` as the likely requirement. Not an outage — `cycsail.team` returns 302 (oauth2-proxy redirect, healthy) and TLS is fine. The running containers still hold the secrets they fetched at their last successful boot, in `/var/substrate/substrate.env`. The breakage is confined to `substrate-apply` at deploy time.

input.command:
cd /Users/ungood/workspaces/personal/isthmia/.claude/worktrees/program-catalog; gh issue create --title "substrate-runner lost secretAccessor on eight secrets and pulumi up will not restore it" --label bug --label P1 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

`substrate-apply` fails on every `pulumi up`. The VM reaches Secret Manager and is refused:

```
GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID is empty; secret fetch failed
```

```
$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" .../google-oauth-client-id/versions/latest:access
403 Permission 'secretmanager.versions.access' denied on resource
```

The VM runs as `substrate-runner@`. Its IAM policy on those secrets is **empty** — not wrong, absent:

```
$ gcloud secrets get-iam-policy google-oauth-client-id --format=json
{ "etag": "BwZbZhASpTc=", "version": 1 }
```

Confirmed empty on `google-oauth-client-id`, `google-oauth-client-secret`,
`portal-oauth-cookie-secret` and `directus-db-password`. All four carry sequential `BwZbZhA…`
etags, so they were cleared in one batch. `clubspot-sync-directus-token`, which is granted to a
different service account, still has its binding (`BwZbYvp…`) — so whatever did this was scoped to
`substrate-runner`'s grants, not to every secret.

By the code, `substrate-runner` should hold `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on eight secrets:
`google-oauth-client-id`, `google-oauth-client-secret`
(`packages/infrastructure/src/infrastructure/substrate.ts:25-27`), `portal-oauth-cookie-secret`
(`portal.ts:25`), and `directus-key`, `directus-secret`, `directus-db-password`,
`directus-admin-bootstrap-password`, `directus-license-key` (`directus.ts:46-54`).

**The deploy cannot heal this.** Pulumi's state still holds those `SecretIamMember` resources, so
`pulumi up` reports them unchanged (`92 unchanged` across two runs today) and never re-creates the
bindings. State and reality disagree and nothing reconciles them.

**It also went unnoticed for ten days.** `substrate-apply` only runs when the compose content hash
or image URL changes (`substrate-apply.ts:31`). The last successful run was 2026-09-13; the next
attempt, on 2026-09-23, failed. Nothing between those dates would have reported it.

No outage: the containers hold the values they fetched at their last successful boot, and
`cycsail.team` still serves. Only deploys are blocked.

## Fix

Restore the eight bindings:

```sh
for s in google-oauth-client-id google-oauth-client-secret portal-oauth-cookie-secret \
         directus-key directus-secret directus-db-password \
         directus-admin-bootstrap-password directus-license-key; do
  gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding "$s" \
    --member="serviceAccount:substrate-runner@cyc-admin-scripts.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"
done
```

Then work out how this class of drift gets caught:

- Find what removed them. Check Cloud Audit Logs for `SetIamPolicy` on those secret resources
  around the etag change. Until that is known, a restore may simply be undone again.
- Decide whether `just deploy` should refresh first, or run a drift check. `just refresh` exists
  but is not part of `deploy`, and refreshing a stack holding the `Directus*` dynamic resources
  needs thought before it becomes routine — related to #126, which is the same shape one layer up
  (apply verification that does not check everything it applied).
- Consider a preflight in `apply.sh` that names the missing grant rather than reporting an empty
  variable. The current message says a secret fetch failed but not that it was a 403, which is what
  made this take a while to place.

## Impact

Every deploy that touches the compose stack or the substrate image fails, and the failure mode
points at the wrong thing — the script reports an empty variable while the real cause is a missing
IAM binding. The ten-day gap between breaking and being noticed is the more serious half: nothing
watches for the running configuration drifting away from what the IaC declares.

content.text:
Now I have the full sequence for `google-oauth-client-id`:

| When | Action | Policy written |
|---|---|---|
| 09-09 22:35 | `CreateSecret` | — |
| 09-09 22:36 | `SetIamPolicy` | **with** `substrate-runner` |

An empty-bindings write is the removal of the last member, i.e. a **delete** of the `SecretIamMember`. But state still holds the resource. Both can only be true if these were **replaced** — Pulumi created the new member, then deleted the old one, and since `SecretIamMember` is read-modify-write against one shared policy, the delete undid the create. State records the new resource as live; GCP ends up empty. That's the classic Pulumi IAM replacement footgun, and it explains every observation including why `pulumi up` sees no diff.

input.command:
cd /Users/ungood/workspaces/personal/isthmia/.claude/worktrees/program-catalog; gh issue comment 153 --body "## Root cause found in the audit log

Full \`SetIamPolicy\` history for \`google-oauth-client-id\`:

| When (UTC) | Action | Policy written |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-09-09 22:35:46 | \`CreateSecret\` | — |
| 2026-09-09 22:36:18 | \`SetIamPolicy\` | **with** \`substrate-runner\` |
| 2026-09-09 22:46:24 | \`AddSecretVersion\` | value set out of band |
| 2026-09-13 20:12:26 | \`SetIamPolicy\` | **with** \`substrate-runner\` |
| 2026-09-13 21:49:23 | — | \`substrate-apply\` succeeds — binding still present |
| **2026-09-13 23:56:14** | \`SetIamPolicy\` | **empty, no bindings** |

The 23:56 write was Pulumi, not a person:

\`\`\`
callerSuppliedUserAgent: \"Pulumi/3.0 (GPN:Pulumi; https://www.pulumi.com) pulumi-gcp/v8.41.1\"
principalEmail:          ungood@onetrue.name
request.policy:          { \"etag\": \"BwZbYu+v3RI=\" }      <- no bindings
response.etag:           \"BwZbZhASpTc=\"
\`\`\`

That response etag is byte-identical to what the secret carries today, so nothing has touched it since. The same second shows the same empty write against \`google-oauth-client-secret\`, \`portal-oauth-cookie-secret\`, \`directus-key\`, \`directus-secret\`, \`directus-db-password\`, \`directus-admin-bootstrap-password\` and \`directus-license-key\`.

### Why state and reality disagree

\`pulumi stack export\` still holds all eight resources, e.g.
\`secret-accessor-google-oauth-client-id-substrate-runner\`. State says present; GCP says empty; \`pulumi up\` therefore sees no diff and reports \`92 unchanged\`.

An empty-bindings write is the removal of the last member — a **delete**. A delete whose resource is still in state is the signature of a **replacement**: Pulumi created the new \`SecretIamMember\`, then deleted the old one. Because \`SecretIamMember\` is read-modify-write against a single shared IAM policy, the delete's read happened after the create and removed the member the create had just added. Net result: state records the new resource as live, the policy ends up empty.

This is the well-known Pulumi/Terraform IAM-member replacement hazard, and it will recur on any future replacement of these resources — a change to \`secretId\`, \`project\`, \`role\` or \`member\` forces one.

### Revised fix

1. Restore the eight bindings by hand (commands in the issue body). Nothing else recovers them, since \`pulumi up\` sees no work to do.
2. Set \`deleteBeforeReplace: true\` on the \`SecretIamMember\` in \`Secret.grant()\` (\`packages/infrastructure/src/infrastructure/secret.ts:28-35\`). Delete-then-create leaves the create as the last writer, so a replacement converges on the right policy instead of an empty one.
3. Consider whether \`grant()\` should return an authoritative \`SecretIamBinding\` per (secret, role) instead of a non-authoritative member. Fewer moving parts when a secret has exactly one grantee, which is the case for all eight here.

The ten-day detection gap stands as written: \`substrate-apply\` only runs when the compose hash or image URL changes, so nothing exercised these grants between 09-13 and 09-23." 2>&1 | tail -2

Worth keeping in mind from #153: **`deleteBeforeReplace` doesn't repair drift, only prevents it.** The plan showed no `SecretIamMember` changes at all, so if this happens again the symptom will be the same — a deploy that fails on a secret fetch while `pulumi up` cheerfully reports everything unchanged. The audit-log query is the way to spot it:

```sh
gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.serviceName="secretmanager.googleapis.com" AND protoPayload.methodName:"SetIamPolicy"' \
  --freshness=45d --format="value(timestamp, protoPayload.resourceName, protoPayload.request.policy.bindings)"
```

An empty third column is a wipe.

Directus holds the canonical model, and each SaaS product gets a sync package that maps it onto
one or more app domains. The rule that follows: **a canonical collection describes the org, and
anything specific to one product is owned by that product's package.** "Fred is a Parent
Coordinator of J-Pod" is canonical, in `crm`. "Anyone holding a program role is a member of that
program's Google Group" is `gsuite-sync`'s own mapping.

A provider may add a field to a collection it doesn't own: `programs.google_group_id` is a real
column on `programs`, declared in `gsuite-sync`'s `schema.yaml`, not `crm`'s. `directus` extends
`people` the same way, for `people.directus_user_id`. The rule cuts by collection ownership, not
by which package is canonical: a field on a `clubspot` collection declared elsewhere would be an
extension too.
